title: The Metaphysics in modern English
author: Aristotle
label: The Workshop's modern English, machine-assisted: drafted with an AI model (Claude) and not yet checked by a scholar. The Greek of each paragraph, and Taylor's English of each chapter, are one tap away.
about: A modern English version of Aristotle's Metaphysics, written for the Workshop, a few books at a time: so far Books Α, α, Β and Γ (I to IV). It modernises the public-domain English on the shelf, W. D. Ross's in the Oxford translation (1908), checked sentence by sentence against the Greek, Ross's own later text (Oxford, 1924) as Perseus gives it; where the old English and the Greek differ, the modern version follows the Greek. It is compared with Thomas Taylor's translation (1801), the English the Platonists' Workshop reads beside it: where an older English says something the Greek does not, or the Greek is hard, a flag shows the older words and the difference. The books and chapters are Bekker's; the short titles and summaries are the Workshop's. Taylor divides Book Α into seven chapters, not ten, and Book Γ into seven, not eight, so each chapter names the chapter of his that holds it. The Platonists read the Metaphysics last of Aristotle's works, as the summit of the course: the science of the first causes and principles, which Aristotle calls wisdom and theology.

treatises.title: Metaphysics, Book Α (I)
treatises.summary: The Metaphysics is the work the Platonists read last of Aristotle's, as the summit of the course: the science of the first causes and principles, which Aristotle calls wisdom, first philosophy and theology. Book Α opens the inquiry. All men by nature desire to know; knowledge rises from the senses through memory and experience to art and science, and wisdom is the knowledge of the first causes, sought for its own sake, the most divine of the sciences (chapters 1 and 2). There are four causes: the matter, the source of motion, the form or what it is to be, and the end (3). Aristotle then reviews the earlier thinkers, to see whether they found any cause beyond these four: the first philosophers found only the material cause; others added a source of motion, love and strife, or intellect; the Pythagoreans made number the principle; the Eleatics made the whole one (3 to 5). Plato's philosophy, the Forms, the great and the small and the One, is set out (6), and the review is summed up (7). Then come the objections: to the materialists and the Pythagoreans (8), and at length to the Forms (9), where Aristotle speaks as one of Plato's school ("we"). The book closes by saying that all the earlier thinkers sought these four causes, but dimly, as a child lisps (10).

treatises.title: Metaphysics, Book α (II), the "little alpha"
treatises.summary: A short book, perhaps a separate lecture, placed between Α and Β, and named in the ancient lists "little alpha". It is about the study of truth in general. The truth is hard to reach as a whole but easy in part, and we owe thanks even to those who erred, since they trained us; philosophy is rightly called knowledge of the truth, and the principles of eternal things are most true (chapter 1). There is no infinite series of causes of any of the four kinds: there must be a first cause, or there would be no cause, no end, no knowledge (2). Finally, how one is to listen and learn: each kind of argument has its own exactness, and mathematical exactness is not for natural things (3).

treatises.title: Metaphysics, Book Β (III)
treatises.summary: Book Β is the book of puzzles (aporiai). Before looking for the science of the first causes, Aristotle says, one must go through the difficulties, as one must see a knot before untying it. He lists some fourteen of them (chapter 1) and argues each both ways (2 to 6): whether one science studies all four causes, the starting-points of proof, and all substances, with their attributes; whether there are substances besides sensible things, such as Forms and the objects of mathematics between them; whether the principles are the genera or the parts a thing is made of, and, if genera, the highest or the lowest; whether anything is apart from individual things; whether the principles are one in kind or in number, and whether perishable and imperishable things have the same principles; whether being and the One are the substance of things, as Plato and the Pythagoreans said; whether numbers, solids, surfaces and points are substances; and whether the principles are universal or individual, and in potency or actual. The book answers none of them; the later books do (Γ, Ζ to Θ, Λ, Μ and Ν). For the Platonists it is the book where Aristotle's quarrel with Plato is set out as a set of fair questions, several of which Syrianus answers in his commentary on Books Β and Γ.

treatises.title: Metaphysics, Book Γ (IV)
treatises.summary: Book Γ answers the first puzzles of Book Β. There is a science of being as being, and of what belongs to it as such (chapter 1). "Being" is said in many ways, but all of them with reference to one thing, substance, as everything healthy is called so with reference to health; so one science studies all that is, and above all substance, and with it the one and the many, same and other, the contraries, and the rest (2). The same science, first philosophy, studies the axioms of all proof, and the firmest of them: that the same thing cannot at the same time belong and not belong to the same thing in the same respect, the principle of non-contradiction (3). It cannot be proved, since it is the starting-point of all proof, but it can be defended by refutation against anyone who will say something that means something (4). Aristotle then answers Protagoras' "man is the measure", the Heracliteans' flux and those who think everything that appears is true (5 and 6), and shows that there is nothing between a contradiction's two sides, the principle of the excluded middle (7), and that neither everything is true nor everything false, nor are all things at rest or all in motion: there is a first mover, itself unmoved (8). For the Platonists the defence of the axioms against Protagoras and the flux follows Plato's Theaetetus, which Aristotle often echoes.

chapters.title: From the senses to wisdom
chapters.summary: All men by nature desire to know, as their love of the senses shows. From sense comes memory, from many memories experience, and from experience art and science. Experience knows that something is so; art knows why, and so can teach. Wisdom is knowledge of causes and principles, and the more theoretical a knowledge, the more it is wisdom.

taylor.label: Book I, Chapter 1
taylor.text:
XIlLI' nien naturally desire to know; a token of which Is the love of the senses ; for, separate from utility, they are loved for themselves, and this is especially the case with the sense of seeing. For, as I may say, we choose to see, in preference to every thing else, not only that we may ad, but likewise when we have no intention of acting. But the cause is, that this sense in a most eminent degree makes us to know something, arid renders many differences manifest. Animals therefore are produced naturally possessing sense. But from sense, in some of them memory is not ingenerated, and in others it is. And on this account, some animals are prudent, but others are more capable of discipline than those who are not able to exercise the power of memory. Those indeed are prudent without discipline, who are unai)Iar to hear loutids, luch as bees, and other animnls oi this kind, if any such are to be found. But those learn, vvlio tt'gether with memory possess the sense of hearing. Other animals therefore live from phantasy, and memory, and participate but a Uttle of experience ; but the human race Uvcs from art also, and veafoning. But men derive experience from memory. For memory being often exercised aliout the same thing, gives perfection to the power of one experience. Hence .experience appears to be nearly hmilar to science and art. But science and art proceed to men through experience. For experience, as Pokis f rightly observes, produces art, but u ifkilfulnefs chance. But art is then effected, when, {rom many conceptions of experience, one universal opinion about things similar is produced. For to have an opinion that to Callias, Socrates, and to many otheis levtrally considered, laboring under a cenain disease, this particular thing is expedient, is the province of experience ; but thit it is expedient to al! of this kind who are denned according to one fpe se?, and who are afflicted with this dileafe, such as 'he phlegmatic, or the choleric, or thnfe who are in a 'ever from heat, is the prr^viuce of art.

With respect therefore to acting. expe-fence seems in no respect to differ from art ; but we fte that the fkiliul more readily accomplish what they mtcnd, than those who possess the reason of a thing with' ut experience. But the cause of this is, that experience is a knowledge of particulars, but art of tning^ univerlal. But all actions and generations are about that which is particular. For he who cures does not give health to man, unless by accident, ^^ut to Callias or Socrates, or some one of others who are thus denomina'ed, and who happens to be a man. If any one therefore possesses the reason of a thing without experience, and know\s indeed that which is universal, but is ignorant of the individual it contains, he will often err in his attempts to cure. For that which is particular polleflls a greater capability of being cured ; but at the same time we are of opinion that to know, and to understand, btlong rather to art than to experience, and we think that artists are wiler than the experienced, because in all men wisdom is rather the consequence of knowledge thanof any thing tlfe. But this takc^ place, because some know, and others do not know the cause of a thing. For the st-iilful indeed know that a thing is, but they do not know ivhy it is ; but the scientific know the lahy and the cause ( f a thing. On this account we consider those who in any thing are master artists, as more honrrable, as those who know more than manual operate rs, and likewise as more wise, because they know the causes of things which are ma<le. But others, like certain inanimate beings, make indeed, but make destitute of knowledge, just in the same manner as tire burns. Inanimate beings, therefore, make each of these things by a certain nature; but manual artificers through custom ; as being wiser, not from their engaging in active pursuits, but from their possessing reason, and knowing the causes of things. And, in ihorr, it is a lign that a man pcffefTes knowledge, when he is able to teach ; and on this account we think that art is more science than experience : for the former are able, but the latter are not able, to teach.

Further still, we do not think that any one of the senses iswifdom, although each is the most: principal knowledge of particulars ; but the senses do not assert the why respecting any thing, as for instance, -dohy fire is hot, but only that it is hot. It is probable, therefore, that the firfi: inventor of any art, besides the common senses, was admired by men, not only because something of things invented was useful, but as being wise and differing from other men. But ■when many arts were discovered, some of which pertain to things neceffiry, but others to the conduft of life, from that time we have always considered those who know the causes of things as wiser than manual artificers, because their sciences do not regard utility. Hence all such things as contribute to the common purposes of life being procured, those sciences were invented, wl'.ieh neither respect pleasure nor things neceffarv, and they were first discovered in thole places in which men abounded in leifiire. On which account the mathematical arts first originated about Kgypt ; for there the tribe of priests was permitted to be at leiliiie. In our moral treatises f, therefore, we have have declared what the difference is between art and science, and other things of a kindred nature. But that for the sake of which we engage in the present discourse, is the belief of all mankind, that what is called wisdom, is conversant with first causes and principles. So that, as we before ohferved, the ikilful man appears to be wiser than those who merely energize from any one of the senses ; the artist: than the skilful ; the architect than manual artificers; and the theoretic than fabricators. That wisdom, therefore, is a science about certain causes and principles, is evident.

chapters.title: What wisdom is: the science of the first causes
chapters.summary: From what we think of the wise, wisdom must be the most universal, exact and authoritative knowledge, sought for its own sake: knowledge of first principles and causes, among them the good. Philosophy began in wonder, as a free science, not for use. It is the most divine science, both because God would have it and because it is about God; it ends, unlike our first wonder, in knowing why things must be as they are.

taylor.label: Book I, Chapter 2
taylor.text:
But, fmce we investigate this science, we should consider from the speculation of what causes and principles science is wisdom. If any one therefore shall apprehend the opinions which we entertain respecting a wise man, perhaps from this the thing proposed will become more evident. In the first place then, we are of opinion, that a wise man in the most eminent degree knows scientifically all that can be known ; not possessing a science of things according to that which is particular, but according to that which is universal. In the next place, we consider him as a wise man, who is able to know things difficult, and which it is not easy for man to know. For, to perceive according to sense is common to all men ; on which account this is easy, and he who thus energizes is by no means wise. In the third place, we are of opinion, that he who is more accurate, and more capable of teaching the causes of things, is more wise respecting every science. Further still, that of sciences, that which is eligible for its own sake, and for the sake of knowing, partakes more of wisdom than that which is eligible for the sake of things which are contingent ; and that the more principal science partakes more of wisdom than that which is subservient. For it is not proper that the wise man Should be commanded, but that he should command ; nor ought he to be persuaded by another, but one less wise ought to be persuaded by him. And such and so many are the opinions which we entertain respecting wisdom and wise men. But, among these, to know all things neceflarlly belongs to him who in the most: eminent degree possesses universal science. For such a one ina certain refpe£t knows all fubjeils. But things most eminently universal are nearly most: difEcuk too for man to know. For they are most remote from the senses. But the most accurate of the sciences are those which especially relate to things first. For those sciences which consist from fewer thinrrs, are more accurate than those which are denominated from addition ; as arithmetic than geometry. But indeed that science is more do£lrinal which speculates the causes of things. For those teach others, who about every thing relate the causes. But to know, and to know scientifically for the sake of such knowledge, especially belongs to the science of that which is most eminently the objeiSl of scientific knowledge. For he who chooses to know scientifically for the sake of such knowledge, especially chooses that which is most eminently science. But such is the science of that which is most eminently the object of scientific knowledge. And objects of this kind are things first and causes. For, through and from these, other things are known, but these are not known through things ih subjection to them. But the most principal of sciences, and which is more a principle than the science which is in fubje<5lion, is that which knows on what account every thing is to be done. But this is the good of every thing ; and universally that which is best in every nature. From all therefore that has been said, that name which is the obje(5l of our investigation falls into the same science. For it is necessary that this ftiould be speculative of first principles and causes. For the good also, and that for the sake of which a thing subsists, is one among the number of causes.

But that this science is not employed in making, is evident from those who first philofophifed. For, both now and at first, men began to philofophife through wonder f : at first indeed admiring such dubious particulars, as were of a more easy solution ; but afterwards proceeding in this manner gradually, they began to doubt about things of greater importance, such as concerning the properties participated by the moon, the sun, and the stars, and the generation of the universe. But he who doubts and wonders, is of opinion that he is ignorant ; and, on this account, a philosopher in a certain respect is a lover of fables. For a fable is cornpofed from things wonderful. So that if now and at first men philofophifed, in order to fly from ignorance, it is evident that they pursued scientific knowledge for the sake of knowing, and not for the sake of any life. But the truth of this is also testified by that which has happened. For nearly all such things as are neceiTary being present, and which contribute both to ease and the conduft of life, prudence of this kind began to be investigated. It is evident therefore, that we seek after scientific knowledge for the sake of no other utility than that which ariles from itself ; and that as we call him a free man who exills for his own sake, and not for the sake of another, so this alone among the sciences is liberal : for tliis alone subsists for its own sake. On this account, too, the possession of it may justly be considered as not human. For in many respects human nature is fei vile ; so that, according to Simonides, divinity alone possesses this honor ; but it is unbecoming that man should only invefligatethe science which pertains to himself :j". But, if the poets say any thing to the purpose, and a divine nature is naturally envious, it is likely that it would especially happen in this particular, and that all those would be unhappy who surpass the rest of mankind. But neither does a divine nature admit of envy ; and poets (according to the proverb) speak falsely in many things.

Nor is it proper to think that any other science is more honorable than a science of this kind. For that which is divine is also most honorable. But a thing of this kind will alone subsist twofold. For the science which divinity poffcffcs is especially divine ; and this will likewise be the case with the science of things divine , if there be such a science. But the science of which we are ipcaking alone possesses both these prerogatives. For divinity appears to be a cause and a certain principle to all things ; and either alone, or in the mod eminent degree, divinity possesses such a science as this. All other sciences therefore are more ntceffiry, but no one is better than this. But it is requisite in a certain respect to eftabllQi this science in an order contrary to that of the inquiries which men made from the beginning. For all men, as we have said, begin from wonder to investigate the manner in wlilch a thing subsists ; just as it happens to those, who have not yet contemplated the cause of thole wonderful llgures that move spontaneously, or the cause of the revolutions of the sun, or the reufon of the incommenfurabiiity of the diameter of a square to the side. For it seems admirable to all men, that a thing which is not the least of things, should not be measured. But it is requisite they should end in the contrary, and in that which is better, according to the proverb, as is the case in these things when they learn them. For there is not any thing which would appear more wonderful to a geometrician, than if the diameter should become commensurable to the side. And thus we have declared what the nature is of that science which is the objeft of our investigation, and what the mark to which the inquiry and the whole method ought to be directed.

chapters.title: The four causes, and the first philosophers on matter
chapters.summary: The causes are spoken of in four ways: the substance, what it is to be; the matter, the underlying thing; the source of motion; and that for the sake of which, the good. The first philosophers saw only the material cause (water for Thales, air, fire, the four elements, Anaxagoras' infinitely many). The facts themselves then drove them to seek the source of motion, and at last intellect, as the cause of order and beauty.

taylor.label: Book I, Chapter 3
taylor.text:
But, since it is evident that it is requisite to consider the science of causes from its principle (for we then say that each particular is known when we know the first: cause of it), and causes are said to iubfift in a fourfold refpc£t, one of which we assert to be efeiicc'-'^, and the fubfilHng as a certain particular thing (for the inquiry. On what account a thing exists, is referred to the last reason f) and cause and principle form the first ivby : but a second cause is ;»i^//fr ; and th:it v/hich fubfiRs as a subject: a third is that ivhence the beginning of motion is derived : but the fourth is the cause oppolite to this, thei for the sake of which a thing fubffs, and the good (for this is the end of all gtnerationj. This being the case, though we have speculated sufficiently concerning these causes In our Physics, yet, at the same time, we Shall take along with us In our inquiry those who prior to us have engaged in the speculation of beings, and have philofophifed about truth. For it is evident that they also assert that there are certain principles and causes. A repetition, therefore, of what they have said will be of advantage to the present discussion. For, either we shall find another genus of cause, or we shall more firmly believe those we have just now enumerated.

The greater part then of those that first philofophifed were of opinion that the principles of all things alone subsisted in the species of matter. For that from which all things subsist, from which they are first generated, and into which they are finally corrupted, the essence indeed remaining but becoming changed by participations, this, say they, is the element, and this is the principle, of things. Hence they were of opinion that neither is any thing generated nor corrupted, because this nature Is always preserved. Just as we say that Socrates Is neither simply generated, when he becomes beautiful, or a musician, nor is corrupted when he loses these habits, because the subject, Socrates himself, remains ; in like manner, neither is any one of other things, either generated, or corrupted. For It Is requisite there should be a certain nature, either one, or more than one, from which other things are generated while it Is Itself preserved.

But with respect to the multitude and form of this principle, all philosophers do not all'ert the same. For Thales indeed, who was the leader of this philosophy, said that this principle is water. On this account he asserted that the earth is placed upon water, entertaining perhaps this opinion from seeing that the nutriment of all things was moist, that the hot itself was generated from this, and that from this animals lived. But that from which any thing is generated Is the principle of that thing. On this account, therefore, he formed this opinion, and because the seeds of all things have a moist nature. But water is the principle of nature to things moist. But there are some who think that men of the greatest antiquity, who flourlfhed long before the present generation, and who first theologized, entertained the very same opinion respecting nature. For they made Ocean f and Tethys the parents of generation, and the solemn oath of the gods water, which Is called Styx by the poets. For that which is the most: antient is the most honorable : but a ft)lcmn oath is the most. honorable. That this opinion, therefore, respecting nature is very antient, is perhaps not immanifefl:. Thales indeed is said to have discoursed in this manner respecting the first; cause. For no one v\'ill think that Hippo deserves to be ranked with these, on account of the meanness of his cogitative part "f. Anaximenes and Diogenes placed air prior to water, and considered it as in the most eminent degree the piinJple of simple bodies. Hippafus the Mctapontine, and Heraclitus the Fphefian, considered lire as the principle of all tilings. But F.mpedocles, who introduced four princip'es, besides those already mentioned added earth for the fourth. For according to him these always remain, and are not generated, but are mingled and separated in multitude and paucity, into one, and from one. But Anaxagoras the Clazomenian, who was prior in age to Empedocles, but posterior in his works, asserts that there are infinite principles. For he says, that nearly all things which consist of similar parts, such as water or fire, are thus generated and corrupted by concretion and separation alone ; but that otherwise they are neither generated nor corrupted, but remain as things eternal. From these men, therefore, any one might be led to think that cause alone belongs to that which is called the species of matter. But in consequence of their proceeding in this manner, the thing itself afforded them a passage, and compelled them to investigate. For though every corruption and generation is in the most eminent degree, from something, as subsisting from one, or from many things ; yet, why does this happen, and what is the cause of it ? for the subject itself does not make itself change. I say, for instance, that neither wood nor brass is the cause that either of these is changed. Nor does wood make the bed, nor brass the statue, but something else, which is the cause of mutation. But to investigate this is to investigate another principle, which we should call that from whence motion derives its beginning. Those, therefore, who have entirely touched upon this method from the beginning, and who assert that the fubje£t is one, have not rendered any thing in this inquiry difficult to themselves ; but some of those who assert that all things are one, as if vanquiftied by this Inquiry, assert that the one is immoveable, and likewlfe the whole of nature, not according to generation and corrugation (for this is an antient opinion, and acknowledged by all men), but alio according to every other mutation. And this is the peciili;iritv of trieir dodrine.

Of those, therefore, who assert that the universe Is alone one, it has so happened that no one has perceived a cause of this kind, except Purmenides j and this has h:mpened to him so far as he admits that there is not only one, but, in a certain respect:, two causes. But to those who admit that there are more than two causes, it belongs in a still greater degree to assert a cause of this kind ; such as those who consider as causes the hot and the cold, or fire ar.d earth. For they ule fire as poifefrmg a motive natuie ; but water and earth, and things of this kind, as endued with a nature contrary to the motive. But after these and such I ke principles, as not being luflicient to generate the nature of things, again, being compelled, as we have said, by truth, they invelligated th;it principle which is consequent to this. For perhaps neither earth, nor any other llmilar nature, is the cause that feme things subsist, and that others are generated in a good and beautiful manner, nor is it probable that they entertained such an opinion. Nor, again, is it proper to ascribe a ihlnr' of such great importance to chance and fortune. He f therefore who asserted asserted that as in animals, so also in namre, there is a certain lntelle<fl, which is the cause both of the world, and of all order, will appear like one sober, when compared with those antients that spoke rashly. We evidently know, therefore, that Anaxagoras touched upon these reasons ; though Hermotimus the Clazomenian is said prior to him to have mentioned a cause of this kind. Those, therefore, who entertained this opinion, together with establishing a principle of things, which is the cause of their subsisting in a beautiful manner eftabliihed also a principle which is the cause of motion to things.

chapters.title: Love and strife; the atomists
chapters.summary: Hesiod and Parmenides may have looked for a moving cause first, in love. Since there is evil as well as good in nature, Empedocles made two, love and strife, in a way the first to make the good and the bad principles. But these thinkers used their causes like untrained boxers, by chance: Anaxagoras brings in intellect only when at a loss. Leucippus and Democritus made the full and the empty the elements, and their differences of shape, order and position the causes of everything else; motion they neglected.

taylor.label: Book I, Chapter 4
taylor.text:
But some one may' fufpecSt that Hesiod first invefllgated a thing of this kind ; and likewise that this is the case with any other who may have considered love or desire as a principle in beings, such, for instance, as Parmenides. For he also, devifmg the generation of the universe, says : " He produced Love the first of all the gods." But Hesiod, " Chaos was generated the firil of all things; but afterwards wide-bosomed Earth, and Love who excels among all the Immorrals:" as if it were fit that there fiiould be a certain cause in beings whiv:h moves and comprehends things, and binds them together. With refoeiTt to these, therefore, we may be permitted afterwards to judge, which of them ought to rank as the hrft. But fmce the contraries to things good appear alio to be inherent in nature, and not only order .ind the beautitul, but disorder and the base ; and, fmce things evil are more in number than such as are good, hence a certain other philosopher has introd\ic&<\ frietidjijip andjiri/e, each, according to him, being the cause of evil and good. For, if any one should follow and receive this dodrine in that part of his nature which reasons fcientihcally, and not according to what Empedocles f has flammering!y asserted, he will find that friendship is the cause of things good, but strife of things evil. So that, if any one should say that Empedocles in a manner asserts, and is the first who asserts, that good and evil are principles, he will perhaps speak well ; fmce good is the cause of all things that are good, and evil of such as are evil. These, therefore, as we have said, thus far touched upon those two causes which we have defined in our Physics ; I mean the material cause, and that whence motion is derived: but yet they have touched upon these causes obscurely, and in no refpe£t cleaily, but just in the same miniier as those do, who are unexerciied in battles. For these advancing tow:!rds their opponents often strike excellent blows; but neither do these strike from science, nor do those seem to know what they assert. For they do not scarcely in any refpciS: appear to use these principles, except in a Tmall degree. For Anaxagoras uses intellect as a rr,achine to the fabrication of the world, [ just as the gods are introduced in tragedies, when very difficult circumstances take place ;] and, when he doubts on what account it necessarily is, he introduces it by force. But, in other things, he considers every thing else rather than intellect as the cause of generated natures f. And Empedocles indeed uses causes more than Anaxagoras ; but yet neither sufficiently, nor in these does he find that which is confentaneous. For in many places, according to him, frieiiJ/hlp separates, and Jirife mingles things together. For when the universe through Jlrife is separated into the elements, then fire, and each of the other elements, is mingled into one. But when all things through fr'tendfiip accord in one, it is necessary that the parts from each should be again separated. Empedocles therefore, in this refpecft, differing from those who were prior to hirp, was the first: that, by making a division, introduced this cause ; not making one principle of motion, but such principles as are different and con'rary. Further still, he was the firfi: who asserted that the elements which are considered as belonging to the species of matter, are four; yet he dues not use them as four, but as if they were alone two. For he uses fire indeed by itself, but its opposites, earth, air and water, as if they were one nature. But of this any one may be convinced, by considering his verses. He, therefore, as we have said, speaks in this manner, and asserts that there are so many-principles.

But Leucippus, and his associate Democritus, aiTert that the elements of things are ih.e full and the void; affirming that the former is being, and the latter non-being. And again of these, they call the full and the solid being, but the void and the rare non-being. On this account they say that being has not any more subsistence than non-being, because neither has void less subsistence than body. But these are the causes of beings as matter. And, just as those who make the fubj:<St essence of things to be one, generate other things from the participations of this subject, and establish the rare and the dense as the principles of participations ; in the same manner these also assert, that diversities are the causes of other things. But they say that these are three : figure, order, and position. For they assert that being differs by ryfmox, diathege, and trope : but of these ryfmos is figure, diathege order, and trope position : for the letter a differs from the letter n in figure, but the syllable an from na in order, and Z from N in position. But these men, in a manner similar to others, negligently omit to consider with refpeit to motion, whence it is derived, and how it lubfifts in beings. And thus far, as we have said, those prior to us appear to have investigated the two causes of things.

chapters.title: The Pythagoreans and the Eleatics
chapters.summary: The Pythagoreans, trained in mathematics, took the principles of numbers for the principles of all things: number is both the matter and the attributes of things, and its elements are the even and the odd, the unlimited and the limited. Some of them set out ten pairs of contraries. The Eleatics, who make the whole one, belong to another inquiry: Parmenides meant one in account, Melissus one in matter, Xenophanes looked to the whole heaven and called the One God. The chapter ends with what can be learned from all of them.

taylor.label: Book I, Chapter 5
taylor.text:
But among these, and prior to these, those who are called Pythagora^ans, and who were the first that applied themselves to mathematics, gave the precedency to these disciplines ; and, in consequence of being nourished in them, were of opinion that these are the principles of all beings. But since among these disciplines numbers are first by nature, and it appeared to them that in numbers more similitudes both to things which are, and to things in generation, are seen, than in fire, earth, and water (for this particular property f of numbers is justice, that soul and intellect:, and again another opportunity, and in a similar manner, as I may say, with refpeft to each of the rest); and further still, since they perceived the participated properties and reasons ii: of harmonies in numbers, and since other things appeared in every refpe£t to be naturally affimilateu to numbers, but numbers are the first elements of every nature ; hence they conceived the elements of numbers to be the elements of all things, and that all heaven is harmony and number; and such things as are acknowledged to be evinced both in numbers and harmonies, these they collected together and ad;ipted to the participated properties and parts of the heavens, and to the whole order of things. Likewise, if any thing was found any where to be much deficient, they fiipplied the defect, that the whole of their treatise might properly accord with itself. I say for inflauce, since the decad appears to be perfeiV, and to comprehend all the nature of numbers, hence they say that the bodies \^hich revolve in the heavens are ten ; but as nine only are apparent, they make the tenth to be antichthon, or the oppcfite earth. But these things are considered by us more accurately in other places.

However, we have related these th'ngs that we may understand from these men what the principles are which they establish, and how they fall into the above-mentioned causes. For it appears that they also considered number as a principle, as matter to beings, and as participated properties and habits. But they assert that the elements of number are the even and the odd ; and that of these, the one is bounded, but the other infinite ; and that the one is conipofed from both these, because it is both even and odd. They likewise assert that number confirts from the one, and that numbers, as we have said, compose the whole of heaven. But others of these assert that there are ten principles, which are denominated according to co-ordination, viz.

Alcmascn the Crotonian appears to have entertained this opinion: and either he derived this dogma from them, or they from him. For Alcmxon flourished when Pythagoras was an old man. But his dodrine was similar to that of these men. For he says that the multitude of human affairs re

ceives a twofold divlfion (meaning into contrarieties), yet not distinguished as they dirtinguiHi them, but defined in a casual manner : such as white, black ; sweet, bitter ; good, evil ; the small, the great. He therefore spoke indefinitely concerning the rest : but the Pythagoreans declare how many, and what are the contrarieties. Hence thus much may be understood from both, that contraries are the principles of beings ; but from the Pythagoreans we learn the niunber and quality of these principles: yet it is not clearly determined by them how they may be applied to the above-mentioned causes. But they appear to dispose the elements as in the species of matter. For from these, as things inherent, they say that efiTence is composed and fashioned. From these things, therefore, the conceptions of the antients, who asserted that the elements of nature were many, may be sufficiently seen.

But there are some who have discoursed about the universe as if it were one nature : yet all of them have not discoursed after the same manner, neither of that which fubfilb beautifully, nor of that which subsists according to nature. By no means, therefore, does the discourse concerning these men harmonife with the present speculation of causes. For they do not speak like certain phyfiologifi:s, who, supposing be'ng to be one, at the same time generate from the one, as from matter ; but their assertions are of a difi'erent nature. For the phyfiologifls who contend that being is one, when they generate the universe, at the same time add motion : but these men assert that the universe is immoveable. Tiius far, however, a discourse about these men is adapted to the present inquiry. For Parmenides appears to have touched upon the one according to reason, but IVlelifliis according to matter. Hence the former afllrts that the universe is finite, but the latter that it is infinite. But Xenophanes, DookL ar [stotle's metappiy si ES, 17 phaiies, who was the first that iiltrcduced this dodtnne (sur Parmenides is said to have been his disciple), did not assert any thing clearly ; nor does he appear to have apprehended the nature of either of these, but, looking to the whole of heaven, he says that (be one is God. These men, therefore, as we have said, are to be difmiifed in the present inquiry ; two of them, iftdeed, entirely, as being a little too ruRic, viz. Xenophanes and Melissus. But Parmenides appears to have seen more than these where to speak. For, befules being itself, he thought fit to consider non-being as nothing, and hence was necessarily of opinion that being is one, and nothing else ; concerning which dodrine we have spoken more clearly in our Physics. But being compelled to follow the phenomena, and conceiving that, according to reason, the one had a subsistence, but, according to sense, the many, he again establishes two causes and two principles, viz. the hot and the cold, or, in other words, fire and earth. But of these he disposes the one, viz. the hot, according to being, but the other according to non being.

From what has been said, therefore, and from those wise men who adhered to reason, we now i^eceive these particulars. From the first indeed, that the limitation of bound. Tliis exception, however, muR be made, that Xenoplianes places it beyond motion and rest, and every anti-ordination, as being the cause of, and transcending, all things, in the same manner as Plato in the first 1-ypothefis of his Parmenides. But Parmenides beholding it as subsisting according to/ntne ^ndjinii/ar (/. e. as having an essence perpetually the same with, and similar to, itself), and as above all mutation, and perhaps energy also and power, celebrates it as immoveable, and alone as being exempt from all things. Meliillis too, in a similar manner, appears to have contemplated the immutability of this cause, and to have evinced that he is /'«finile, as also utihegotten, from the never-failing nature of his essence and th.c infinity of his power."

The opposition, therefore, of Aristotle to the doctrine of these philosophers, is, as usual, direfted to the literal and not to the true meaning of their assertions.

* Arlllotle here means those philosophers who speculated the sensible order of things and investigated the elements of bodies, viz. Thales and Heraclitus, Anaximenes and Diogenes, Anaximander, Leucippus and Democritus. Of these, Thales asserted that the element of bodies was water, in confequencc of surveying its prolific, nutritive, connective, vivific, and yielding nature ; but Heraclitus, that it was fire, from regarding, the vivific and demiurgic nature of this element. Anaximenes affirmed that it was air, from beholding the plastic power of this element, and the facility with which it pervades fire and water; and Anaximander, that it was of a middle nature, between fire and air, from the facility with which it receives mutation. And, lastly, Leucippus and Democritus called the elements of bodies atoms, in consequence of regarding the diflcrcnce of their figures, position, and,order. So that, as SimpHcius justly observes of the antlent philosophers, some contemplated the intelligible, and others the sensible, order of things. Some in-D vcftigated the principle cf tilings is corporeal (for water, and ftre, and the like, are bodies) ; and of these some assert that there is one, but others that there are many corporeal principles ; but both agree in placing these principles as in the Species of matter. But from certain others who establish this cause, we receive besides this the principle whence motion is derived ; and according to some there is one principle, but according to others there are two principles of this kind. As far, therefore, as to the Italic philosophers, and separate from them, others have spoken in a more becoming manner about these things, except, as we have said, that they used two causes ; and of these some made the other cause, or that whence motion is derived, to be one, but others to be two. The Pythagora:ans, after the f.ime manner, said that there are two principles. But thus much they added, which is peculiar to them, that they did not think the finite, and the infinite, and the one were certain other natures, such as fire, or earth, or any other similar thing ; but they were of opinion, that the infinite itself, and the one itself, are the essence of these things of which they are predicated : and hence they asserted that number is the essence of all things. After this manner, therefore, they unfolded their opinion, refpcdling these things, and began to speak about what a thing is, and to define ; but they treated this affair in a very simple manner. For they defined fiiperficially, and confidcred that in which a given definition is first inherent, as the eirence of the thing ; just as if any one lliould think that the double and the duad are the same, because the double first subsists in two. But perhaps the double is not the same with the duad : and if it be not, one thing vrill be many; which consequence happens also to them. From thole, therefore, who first philofophifed, and from others, thus much may be received.

chapters.title: Plato
chapters.summary: Plato followed the Pythagoreans in most things, but had his own views. From Heraclitus he took that sensible things are in flux and cannot be known; from Socrates, the search for definitions; so the definitions must be of other things, the Forms, in which sensible things participate. Between the two are the objects of mathematics. The elements of the Forms are the great and the small as matter and the One as substance, and the Forms are numbers. Aristotle concludes that Plato used only two causes, what it is to be and matter, and gave the cause of good and of evil to his two elements.

taylor.label: Book I, Chapter 6
taylor.text:
After the above-mentioned plulofophers, the business with Plato next fiiccceds, who in many things followed these Pythagorasans, but who also had some peculiar dodrines different from the philoCophy of the Italics. For, when he was a young man, associating first of all with Cratylus, and being familiar with the opinions of Heraclitus, that all sensible things are perpetually flowing, and that there is no science respecting th.m, he afterwards adopted these opinions. But as Socrates employed himself about ethics, find entirely neglected the speculation respecting the whole of nature ; in morals, indeed, investigating the universal, and being the first who applied himfeh to definitions; hence Plato, approving this his investigation of universals, ad.'pted thus much of his dodrine, that these definitions respect other things, and are not conversant with any thing fenfiblc. For he was of opinion, that it is impossible there should be a common definition of any sensible nature, as sensibles are always changing. Things of this kind, therefore, he denominated ideas, but asserted that all sensible things were denominated as different from, and as subsisting according to, these. For, according to him, the multitude of things synonymous is homonymous to forms according to participation ; but he only changed the name participation. For the P) thagorseans say that beings are imitations of numbers ; but Plato, changing the name, calls \\\tm participations of numbers. They omit, however, to invelligate in common what the participation or imitation of forms is. Further Rill, besides things sensible, and forms, they say that the mathematics are things of a middle nature, differing indeed from sensibles in that they are eternal and immoveable, but from forms in that they are certain similar multitudes, every form itself being only one thing. But, since forms are causes to other things, he was of opinion that the elements of these are the elements of beings. He thought, therefore, that the great and the small were principles as matter, but the one \ as essence. For from these, through the participation of the oncy forms are numbers. He asserted, indeed, that the one is essence, and that nothing else is called the one in this respect speaking in a manner similar to the PythagoriEans ; and, like them, he also considered numbers as the causes of essence to other things. But this is pecuhar to him, to make the diiad instead of the iri/in'ite considered as one, and to compose the mjinlte from the great and the small.

Further still : Plato asserts that numbers are different from things sensible ; but the Pythagorseans say that they are things themselves, and do not place mathematics between these. The one, therefore, and numbers, were considered as different from things themselves, and not as the Pythagoreans consider them ; and, as well as forms, were introduced in consequence of dialectic investigation. For the more antient philosophers were not flsiilled in dialectic. Through the same investigation, alio, Plato made the duad to be a different nature from the one, because numbers, except those that rank as first, are aptly generated from it, as from a certain express resemblance of a thing ; though, indeed, the contrary to this happens to be the case. For it is not reasonable it should be so. For now they make many things from matter, but form generates once only. But one table appears to be produced from one matter. However, he who introduces form makes many tables. The male, too, is in a similar manner related to the female. For the female is filled from one copulation, but the male fills many. And yet these are imitations of those principles. Plato, therefore, has thus defined respecting the objecfls of investigation.

But it is evident, from what has been said, that he uses only two causes ; that which relates to what a thing is, and that which subsists according to matter. For forms, accordi-g to liiai, are the causes to other things of essence ; but the o?ie is the cause of this to forms. And what is this cause which lubfifts according to matter? It is that iubje£t matter through which forms are said to belong to things sensible ; and the one is said to be in forms, because this is the duad, or the great and the small. Further still : he attributes lo the elements the cause of subsisting well and ill, each to its proper element; and this, we say, some of the more antient philosophers, viz. Empedocles and Anaxagoras, have investigated. In a brief and summary manner, therefore, we have discussed who those were that have spoken, and how they have fpok 'H, respecting principles and truth. But, at the same time, we obtain thus much from them, that of those-who have spoken concerning a principle and cause, no one has said any thing in addition to what we have delivered in our Physics ; but all of them have spoken obscurely, though in a certain respect they appear to have touched upon these two. For some speak of principle as matter, whether they suppose there is one or many principles, and whether they consider principle as body, or as incorporeal: as Plato, when he speaks oi the great and the f mail -, Empedocles, oi fire and earth, "water and air ; and Anaxagoras, of the infinity offimilar parts. But all these touched upon a cause of this kind ; and, besides these, those who have eflablilhed as a principle eirher lire or water or that which is more dense than fire, but more attenuated than air ; for some assert that the first element is a thing of this kind. These, therefore, had only an obicure conception of this caule ; but certain others had some cnnceptioa whence the principle of motion is derived,, viz. those who make friendlhip and strife, or intellect, or love, a principle. But no one has clearly assigned the nature and essence of this principle. However, they especially speak respecting it who adopt the hypothesis of forms, and the things which subsist in forms. For neither do they consider forms and the things which forms contain as ma'ter to sensibles, nor as if the principle of motion was derived from thence. For they say that they are rather the cause of immobility, and of things being at rest. But, according to them, forms impart the particular being which each individual of other things possesses ; and the one imparts the same to forms. But that, for the sake of which actions, mutations and motions subsist after a certain manner, they denominate a cause; yet they do not assert that it is a cause, nor do they speak of it conformably to what it naturally is. For those who speak of intellect, or friendftiip, place these causes as a certain good, but do not speak of them as if for the sake of these either being or any generated nature f ibfifts, but as if from them the motions of things were derived. In a similar manner, those who say that the one ^ or beings is a nature of this kind, assert indeed that it is the cause of essence ; yet do not say that any thing eiiher is, or is generated, for the sake of this. So that in a certain respect it happens that they assert, and yet do not assert, that the good is a cause of this kind; for they speak not simply, but casually. That we have therefore rightly determined concerning causes, and refpedlng their number and qiafry, all these philosophers appear to testify, since they were not able to touch upon any other cause. And, besides this, that principles should be investigated, either all of them in this manner, or feme one of the four, is evident. But after this it is requifue that we should consider in what manner each of these speaks, and what are the doubts which arise respecting principles themselves.

chapters.title: The review summed up
chapters.summary: None of the earlier thinkers named a cause beyond the four. Some spoke of matter, some of the source of motion; what it is to be was spoken of chiefly by the friends of the Forms; the end they named, but not as an end. So the four causes are rightly set out, and next their views are to be examined.

taylor.text:

chapters.title: Against the materialists and the Pythagoreans
chapters.summary: Those who make one bodily element the principle leave out the bodiless, the source of motion and what things are, and cannot say which element is first. Empedocles has these troubles and more; Anaxagoras, read charitably, means the One and the indefinite. The Pythagoreans use principles fit for higher things to explain only the sensible heaven, and say nothing of how there is motion, weight or lightness, or how number is the cause of the things in the heaven if it is also those things.

taylor.label: Book I, Chapter 7
taylor.text:
It is evident, therefore, that those err manifoldly, who consider the universe as one, and as being one certain nature, as matter ; and this corporeal, and possessing magnitude. For they only admit the elements of bodies, but not of things incorporeal, though at the same time things incorporeal have a fubfiilence. And besides this, endeavouring to assign the causes of generation and corruption, and phyfiologifmg about all things, they take away the cause of motion. Further still, by placing essence as the cause of no one thing, and not considering the isohat \ and besides this, thinking that there might easily be any principle of fmiple bodies (except earth , they did not attend to the manner in which, according to them, the generation of these from each other is accomplilhed ; I mean fire and water, earth and air. For some ■things are generated from each other by concretion, and others by separation. But this, with refpeitto the being prior and posterior, differs much. For that may appear to be the most elementary of all things, from which the elements are generated by a first: concretion : but a thing of this kind will, among bodies, consist of the smallest parts, and be the most attenuated ; on which account, such as place fire as a principle speak in the highest degree conformably to this do£trine. But every one acknowledges that a thing of this kind is also the element of other bodievs. No one, therefore, of those later philosophers who speak oi the one, has thought fit to consider earth as an element, on account of the magnitude of its parts. But each of the three elements has had a certain arbitrator ; for some say that this is fire, others water, and others air. Though why, like the multitude, do they not say that earth also is an element ? fr they say that earth is all things. Hesiod also asserts, that earth was the first thing generated among bodies ; so that this opinion happens to be both aotient and popular. According to this reasoning, therefore, if any one should say that any thing belonging to these, except fire, is more dense than air, but more attenuated than water, he will not speak rightly. But if that which is posterior in generation is prior by nature, and that which is digested and ming'ed together is posterior in generation, the contrary of these will take place ; tor water will be prior to air, and earth to water. And thus much may fuflice rei'petfling thole who establish one cause such as we have mentioned.

But the fixme things may be said, if any one should think that there are many corporeal principles, as Empedocles, who says that the four elementary bodies are matter : for it is necessary that partly the same things, and partly such as are peculiar, should happen to him. For we see that the elements are generated from each other, as the fire and earth of the same body do not always remain. But we have spoken respecting these in our Physics f, and also respecting the cause of things moving, whether it is to be considered as one or two ; nor is it to be thought that this has been asserted in a manner altogether irrational. But, in fine, those whofpeak in this manner must: necessarily take away internal mutation. For the cold is not from the hot, nor the hot from the cold. And what contraries tliemfelves will suffer, and what that one nature will be, which becomes fire and water, Empedocles does not say.

But if any one should think that Anaxagoras asserts there are two elements,. he v/ill, in the highest degree, think according to reason ; for though he does not clearly assert this, yet it follows from necessity, if any one speaks conformably to his doctrine. It is indeed absurd to say, that at first all things were mingled together ; both because it must happen that all things prior to. this ought to have subsisted unmingled, and because every thing is not naturally adapted to be mingled with every thing. To which it may be added, that from this dodrine, parucipated properties and accidents must be separated from substances (for mixture and separation belong to the same things) ; yet if any one follows, and at the same time accurately considers his asses tions, he will perhaps appear to have advanced Ibmething new. For, at the time when nothing was separated, it is evident nothing could be said respecting that essence. I say, for instance, that it was neither white nor black, nor of any colour between these ; but that it was from necessity culourlefs : for other■wife It would possess some one of these colours. In like manner, it must have been tasteless : and, from the same reaibning, it could not have been any thing else of the like land. For it is not poihble that it co\ild possess any-quality or quantity, or be any adual thing, fmce something of those things which are called partial forms would be inherent in it. Cut this is impossible, in conftquence of all things (according to him) being mingled together; for they would now be separated. But he says tiiat all things were mingled except intellect ; and that this alone was unmingled and pin-e. Hence it comes t'l pass, that he proclaims, as principles, the one (for this is simple and unmingled), and another thing, as if it were being, such as we consider the indefinite to be, before it is bounded and participates of a certain form. So that this is afTcited, indeed, neither wish rectitude nor perspicuity ; yet he wufhes to say iomething similar to what more modern philosophers have said, and more agreeable to the prelent phenomena. But the'e philosophers only speak in a manner accommodated to the assertions respecting generation, corruption, and motion. For they nearly alone invefligale an eilence, principles and causes of this kind.

But with respect to such. chapters.title: Against the Forms
chapters.summary: The arguments for the Forms either prove nothing or prove Forms of things the Platonists deny Forms of; the more exact ones lead to Forms of relatives or to the "third man". The Forms explain neither motion nor knowledge nor being; "pattern" and "participation" are empty words and poetic metaphors. If the Forms are numbers, they cannot be causes; the Platonists' account of lines, planes and solids fails; and to seek the elements of all things without distinguishing the senses of being is hopeless. Aristotle speaks here as one of Plato's school ("we").

For thus, perhaps, they might be considered as causes, as a white colour mixed with a body may be said to be the cause that the body is white. But that assertion, which was lirft made by Anaxagoras, and afterwards by Eudoxus and others, respecting the temperament of things from similar natures, may be easily confuted ; for it is eal'y to co11e£l many and impossible confcquences in oppolition to this opinion. Cut, indeed, neither do other things fubfill from, forms, according to any of those modes which are generally adduced. And to say that forms are paradigms, and that they are participated by other things, is to speak vainly, and to utter poetical metaphors. For, v.-hat is that which operates looking to ideas ? for it is possible that any thing may both be, Jfnd be generated similar, without being affnnilated to that to which it is similar; so that, Socrates both subsisting and not subsisting, some other may be generated such as Socrates is : and, in like manner, it is evident that this will follow, although Socrates should be eternal. Besides, there will also be many paradigms of the same thing ; and confequ-Titly forins, as man, animal, biped ; and at the same time, man himlelf, or the ideal ihan, will have a subsistence.

Further still, forms will not only be paradigms of sensibles, but also of forms themselves ; as, for instance, genus, so far as genus, will be the paradigm of species : so that the same thing will be both paradigm and image. Again, it may seem to be impossible that essence Should be separated from that of which it is the essence. So that how will ideas, since they are the essences of things, be separated from them ? But, in the Phiedo, forms are said to be the (.aufes, both that things are, and that they are generated ; though, at the same time, participants will not be generated, even admitting the subsistence of forms, unless that which is motive subsists. And besides this, many other things .".re made, such as a house and a ring, of which we do not say there are forms : so that it is evident that other things may be, and may be generated, through such causes as we have just now mentioned.

Again, if forms are numbers, how will they be causes ? Whether because beings are different numbers ? as, for instance, man is this number, Socrates another, and Callias a number different from both. Why, therefore, are those the causes of these ? For it is of no consequence, if those are eternal, but these not. But if it is because sensible natures are the reasons of numbers, as a symphony, it is evident that there will be one certain thing, of which they are reasons or ratios. If, therefore, this one thing is matter, it is evident that numbers themselves also will be certain ratios of another thingo another thing. I say, for instance, if Callias is a ratio in numbers of fire and earth, water and air, and of certain other subjects, man himself alfa, whether this idea is a certain number or not, will be a ratio of certain things in numbers, without being himself number, and will not through these things be some particular number.

Further still : from many numbers one number is produced ; but how is one form produced from forms ? But if form is not produced from forms, but from the unities which are in number, after what manner will the unities subsist ? For, if they are of the same species, many absurd consequences will ensue ; and if they are not of the same species, nor the same with each other, nor all the rest the same with all, in what do they differ, since they are impassive ? For these things are neither reasonable, nor conformable to intellectual conceptions. Besides, it will likevvife be necessary to eftabliih another ctitain genus of number with which arithmetic must necessarily be conversant ; and all such things as by feme are denominated media. How then do these things subsist, or from what principles do they derive their subsistence ? Or why will they be media between things here and those ? Besides, each of the unities which is in the duad will subsist from a certain something prior to them, viz. the duad itself. This, however, is impossible.

Further still ; since every idea is number, why is it one ? And besides this, if the unities are not • different, it will be requisite to speak in the same manner as those who say that there are four or two elements : for each of these does not call that which is common an element ; as, for instance, body, but Hre and earth, whether body is something common or not. But now the assertion is just as if the one consisted of similar parts, like fire or water j but if this be the case, numbers will not be essences. It is, however, evident, that if the one is any thing, and this is a principle, the o?ie is predicated in a manifold refpe£t ; for it is impossible it should be otherwise. But we, who wifti to reduce essences into principles, assert f that length conlifts from the long and the short, and from the small and the large : that superficies is composed from the broad and the narrow ; and body from the deep and the low. But how can a plane possess a line, or a solid a line and plane ? For the broad and the narrow are a genus different from that of the deep and the low. As, therefore, number is not inherent in these, because the much and the few are different from these, so it is evident that neither will any one of the superior subsist in any of the inferior natures. But neither is the broad the genus of the deep ; for thus body would be a certain superficies.

Again : from what principles will points be composed ? This genus, therefore, Plato opposes, as being a geometrical dogma ; but he calls it the principle of a line; and often asserts that there are indivisible lines, though it is necessary there should be a certain bound of these. So that, for the same reason that there is such a thing as a line, a point also has a fub^iRence. And, in fhorr, since Wiidom investigates the cause of things appa ent, this indeed we omit'''' : for we say nothing refpefting the cause whence the bednning cf mutaiit^n is derived. But, thinking to assign the essence of things apparent, ive foy that there are other essences ; and we in vain describe the manner in which those are the essences of these : for, as we have before obferveJ, it is to no purpose to assert, that this is effected by participation. Nor, again, are id as such causes as we perceive in fciencts, and through which every inicliecl: and every nature produces; nor do t'ey touch upon any cause ■which we lay is one of the principles. But, with thc^fe of the present day, the inattieinatical sciences generated philosophy, though they say it is requisite t ) be conversant with these disciplines for the lake of other things.

Further ftiH, the fuhjtft matter itself f may be considered as being rather mathematical matter, and as that which ought rather to be predicated and to be considered as the difference "f eff^nce and matter, such as the great and the small ; just as phyfiolog'.rts assert that the rare and the dense are the first: ■differences of the subject: matter. For thele are certain excesses and defects. But respecting motion what ought we to thii'k? For if these (viz. excess and defect) are motions it is evident that foru s will be moved : hut if they are not motions, whence is motion derived ? For the whole speculation refj edbing nature will be taken a'^ ay. And befuies this, that which seems to be easy u iii not be accomplished, viz. to demonstrate that all things are one X' For I"or all things do not become one by exposition, but a certain one Itft If, if any one allows all things. Nor yet this, unless he admits that there is an universal genus. But this in certain things is impossible. Nor is there any reason in those things which are posterior to nunbers, viz. lengths, fuperficie? and solids, with refpefl to the mode in v/hich they are or will be ; nor do they poITefs any power. For these can neither be forms (for they are not numbers) nor things ■which have a middle subsistence (for those are mathematical), nor can they be things corrupiible : but again these appear to be a fourth genus, different from those three. And, ia short, it is impossible that any one can fiad hy investigation the elements of beings, unless he divides them, lince they are jnanifoldly predicated ; tfpecially, if he investigates from what eiementi thty are composed. For it is not possible to admit those things from which .adion or passion, or the llraight, consist; but, if it were possible, they could only be admitted as belonging to beings : so that either to investigate, or to think it pc flible to poficfs, the tlements of all beings is not true. For, how can any one learn the elements of all things r fuice it is evident that he cannot pofieis any antecedent knowledge. For, as he who learns geometry may indeed previously know other things, but cannot have a prior knowledge of any of the particulars with which the science of geometry is convcrfant, and in which he is to be instructed ; so likewise in olliLr things. So that, if there ■be a certain science of all tilings, as some af.ert, he who pofrefles this science cannot iiave any pre-existent knowled^je. But yet every diLipliiie subsists through a prior knowledge, either of all things, or of certain particulars ; and is accomplished, either through demonstration or through definitions. For it is requisite that those things should be foreknown from which definition confiRs. And the like takes place with respect to the knowledge which is acquired by indudlon. But if we possess an innate knowledge of things, it is wonderful how we happen to be ignorant that we pollefs the most excellent of sciences'. Further fliil, how can any one know from what particulars all things consist, and how will this be manileft ? For this is dubious: for some one may doubt just as respecting certain syllables, since some assert that the syllable za, is composed from f, d, a f ; but others say it has a different sound, and not any one of those sounds that are known. Again, how can any one, not possessing sense, know sensibles ? yet it is requisite he should, if those are elements of all things, from which things consist, just as composite sounds from their proper elements. From what has been said, therefore, it is evident that all philosophers seem to investigate, though obscurely, those causes which we have spoken of in our Physics, and that we are not able to assign any other cause different from some one of these. For in one refpeA, all these have been mentioned by philosophers prior to us ; but in another refpe(ft they have been by no means mentioned. For the first: philosophy, as being young, and at its first commencement, appears to ftammer about every thing. For Empedocles says, that bone consists from reason (viz. form). But this is the very nature and eflfence of a thing. However, if this were admitted, in like manner flesh, and every thing else, must either be reason or nothing ; for, through this, both flesh and bone, and every other thing, subsist, and not through matter, which he calls fire and earth, and water and air. These things he would necessarily admit, if they were asserted by another person ; but he does not speak clearly respecting them. Things of this kind, therefore, we have rendered manifest before. But such doubts as may arise respecting them we shall again relate ; for, from these, we may perhaps be enabled to solve future doubts. ARISTOTLE'S METAPHYSICS.

chapters.title: All sought the four causes, but dimly
chapters.summary: All the earlier thinkers sought the causes named in the Physics, and no other, but dimly: early philosophy lisps like a child. Empedocles, for instance, said bone is by its ratio, which is what it is to be, but did not say so clearly. The difficulties about these questions come next.

It is evident, therefore, that those err manifoldly, who consider the universe as one, and as being one certain nature, as matter ; and this corporeal, and possessing magnitude. For they only admit the elements of bodies, but not of things incorporeal, though at the same time things incorporeal have a fubfiilence. And besides this, endeavouring to assign the causes of generation and corruption, and phyfiologifmg about all things, they take away the cause of motion. Further still, by placing essence as the cause of no one thing, and not considering the isohat \ and besides this, thinking that there might easily be any principle of fmiple bodies (except earth , they did not attend to the manner in which, according to them, the generation of these from each other is accomplilhed ; I mean fire and water, earth and air. For some ■things are generated from each other by concretion, and others by separation. But this, with refpeitto the being prior and posterior, differs much. For that may appear to be the most elementary of all things, from which the elements are generated by a first: concretion : but a thing of this kind will, among bodies, consist of the smallest parts, and be the most attenuated ; on which account, such as place fire as a principle speak in the highest degree conformably to this do£trine. But every one acknowledges that a thing of this kind is also the element of other bodievs. No one, therefore, of those later philosophers who speak oi the one, has thought fit to consider earth as an element, on account of the magnitude of its parts. But each of the three elements has had a certain arbitrator ; for some say that this is fire, others water, and others air. Though why, like the multitude, do they not say that earth also is an element ? fr they say that earth is all things. Hesiod also asserts, that earth was the first thing generated among bodies ; so that this opinion happens to be both aotient and popular. According to this reasoning, therefore, if any one should say that any thing belonging to these, except fire, is more dense than air, but more attenuated than water, he will not speak rightly. But if that which is posterior in generation is prior by nature, and that which is digested and ming'ed together is posterior in generation, the contrary of these will take place ; tor water will be prior to air, and earth to water. And thus much may fuflice rei'petfling thole who establish one cause such as we have mentioned.

But the fixme things may be said, if any one should think that there are many corporeal principles, as Empedocles, who says that the four elementary bodies are matter : for it is necessary that partly the same things, and partly such as are peculiar, should happen to him. For we see that the elements are generated from each other, as the fire and earth of the same body do not always remain. But we have spoken respecting these in our Physics f, and also respecting the cause of things moving, whether it is to be considered as one or two ; nor is it to be thought that this has been asserted in a manner altogether irrational. But, in fine, those whofpeak in this manner must: necessarily take away internal mutation. For the cold is not from the hot, nor the hot from the cold. And what contraries tliemfelves will suffer, and what that one nature will be, which becomes fire and water, Empedocles does not say.

But if any one should think that Anaxagoras asserts there are two elements,. he v/ill, in the highest degree, think according to reason ; for though he does not clearly assert this, yet it follows from necessity, if any one speaks conformably to his doctrine. It is indeed absurd to say, that at first all things were mingled together ; both because it must happen that all things prior to. this ought to have subsisted unmingled, and because every thing is not naturally adapted to be mingled with every thing. To which it may be added, that from this dodrine, parucipated properties and accidents must be separated from substances (for mixture and separation belong to the same things) ; yet if any one follows, and at the same time accurately considers his asses tions, he will perhaps appear to have advanced Ibmething new. For, at the time when nothing was separated, it is evident nothing could be said respecting that essence. I say, for instance, that it was neither white nor black, nor of any colour between these ; but that it was from necessity culourlefs : for other■wife It would possess some one of these colours. In like manner, it must have been tasteless : and, from the same reaibning, it could not have been any thing else of the like land. For it is not poihble that it co\ild possess any-quality or quantity, or be any adual thing, fmce something of those things which are called partial forms would be inherent in it. Cut this is impossible, in conftquence of all things (according to him) being mingled together; for they would now be separated. But he says tiiat all things were mingled except intellect ; and that this alone was unmingled and pin-e. Hence it comes t'l pass, that he proclaims, as principles, the one (for this is simple and unmingled), and another thing, as if it were being, such as we consider the indefinite to be, before it is bounded and participates of a certain form. For they nearly alone invefligale an eilence, principles and causes of this kind.

But with respect to such. Indeed, as make all beings the subject of their fpeculatlon, and consider some beings as sensible and others as not sensible, it is evident that they inquire concerning both genera ; and on this account any one may be induced to dwell longer on the consideration of what they have said, well or ill, with respect to our present investigation. Further still, whether any one grants them that magnitude is from these, or whether this is shown to be the calc ; yet, at the same time, after what jmanner will some bodies possess levity, and others gravity, relpedling which their hypotheses and axTertions do not less accord with mathematical bodies than with sensibles ? Hence they do not say any thing respecting fire, or earth, or other bodies of this kind; and this, I think, because they do not assert any tiling which is their own concerning sensible natures. For since, according to them, opinion and opportunity are in this part of the worlJ, but a little higher or a little lower, injustice, and separation, or mixture, and they adduce demoaftration that each of these is number, and it happens from this mode of reasoning, that there is now a multitude of constituted magnitudes, because these properties follow the respective places; — since this is the case, whether is it owing to that number which is in the heavens ihat each of these exiRs, or to another number besides this ? I mean, just as if any thing participates of the double, this aho partici[ates of the perpet al, but according to accident. And to say that forms are paradigms, and that they are participated by other things, is to speak vainly, and to utter poetical metaphors. For, v.-hat is that which operates looking to ideas ? for it is possible that any thing may both be, Jfnd be generated similar, without being affnnilated to that to which it is similar; so that, Socrates both subsisting and not subsisting, some other may be generated such as Socrates is : and, in like manner, it is evident that this will follow, although Socrates should be eternal.
