paragraphs.greek: ἡμεῖς δὲ καὶ πρὸς τοῦτον τὸν λόγον ἐροῦμεν ὅτι τὸ μὲν μεταβάλλον ὅτε μεταβάλλει ἔχει τινὰ αὐτοῖς λόγον μὴ οἴεσθαι εἶναι, καίτοι ἔστι γε ἀμφισβητήσιμον· τό τε γὰρ ἀποβάλλον ἔχει τι τοῦ ἀποβαλλομένου, καὶ τοῦ γιγνομένου ἤδη ἀνάγκη τι εἶναι, ὅλως τε εἰ φθείρεται, ὑπάρξει τι ὄν, καὶ εἰ γίγνεται, ἐξ οὗ γίγνεται καὶ ὑφʼ οὗ γεννᾶται ἀναγκαῖον εἶναι, καὶ τοῦτο μὴ ἰέναι εἰς ἄπειρον. ἀλλὰ ταῦτα παρέντες ἐκεῖνα λέγωμεν, ὅτι οὐ ταὐτό ἐστι τὸ μεταβάλλειν κατὰ τὸ ποσὸν καὶ κατὰ τὸ ποιόν· κατὰ μὲν οὖν τὸ ποσὸν ἔστω μὴ μένον, ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὸ εἶδος ἅπαντα γιγνώσκομεν. ἔτι δʼ ἄξιον ἐπιτιμῆσαι τοῖς οὕτως ὑπολαμβάνουσιν, ὅτι καὶ αὐτῶν τῶν αἰσθητῶν ἐπὶ τῶν ἐλαττόνων τὸν ἀριθμὸν ἰδόντες οὕτως ἔχοντα περὶ ὅλου τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ὁμοίως ἀπεφήναντο· ὁ γὰρ περὶ ἡμᾶς τοῦ αἰσθητοῦ τόπος ἐν φθορᾷ καὶ γενέσει διατελεῖ μόνος ὤν, ἀλλʼ οὗτος οὐθὲν ὡς εἰπεῖν μόριον τοῦ παντός ἐστιν, ὥστε δικαιότερον ἂν διʼ ἐκεῖνα τούτων ἀπεψηφίσαντο ἢ διὰ ταῦτα ἐκείνων κατεψηφίσαντο. ἔτι δὲ δῆλον ὅτι καὶ πρὸς τούτους ταὐτὰ τοῖς πάλαι λεχθεῖσιν ἐροῦμεν· ὅτι γὰρ ἔστιν ἀκίνητός τις φύσις δεικτέον αὐτοῖς καὶ πειστέον αὐτούς. καίτοι γε συμβαίνει τοῖς ἅμα φάσκουσιν εἶναι καὶ μὴ εἶναι ἠρεμεῖν μᾶλλον φάναι πάντα ἢ κινεῖσθαι· οὐ γὰρ ἔστιν εἰς ὅ τι μεταβαλεῖ· ἅπαντα γὰρ ὑπάρχει πᾶσιν. —
notes: The region round us: the world below the moon, where things come to be and perish; above it the heavens move eternally and unchangingly (On the Heavens I.3). The Platonists drew the same contrast in Plato's Timaeus and Phaedo (109b-111c).

paragraphs.modern: About the truth, that not everything that appears is true: first, even if sensation, at least of what is proper to it, is not false, appearance is not the same as sensation. Then it is fair to wonder whether they are really puzzled whether magnitudes and colours are such as they appear to those far off or to those near, to the healthy or to the sick; whether the heavier things are those that seem so to the weak or to the strong; and whether the true things are those that appear to the sleeping or to the waking. Plainly they do not think so: no one, at any rate, if he supposes one night that he is at Athens when he is in Libya, sets out for the Odeum. Again, about the future, as Plato too says, the opinion of the physician and that of the ignorant are surely not likewise authoritative, about whether someone will get well or not. Again, among the senses themselves, the sense of what is foreign to it and of what is its own, or of what is near to it and what belongs to it, are not of equal weight: of colour sight judges, not taste, and of flavour taste, not sight; and none of them ever says, at the same time and about the same thing, that it is at the same time so and not so. Not even at another time does a sense disagree about the quality, but only about the thing the quality belongs to. I mean, for instance, the same wine might seem, if it changed or the body changed, at one time sweet and at another not sweet; but the sweet, such as it is when it is, has never yet changed, and one is always right about it, and what is to be sweet is of necessity such. Yet all these arguments do away with this: as there is no substance of anything, so nothing is of necessity; for the necessary cannot be in one way and in another, so that if anything is of necessity, it will not be "so and not so".
paragraphs.greek: περὶ δὲ τῆς ἀληθείας, ὡς οὐ πᾶν τὸ φαινόμενον ἀληθές, πρῶτον μὲν ὅτι οὐδʼ εἰ ἡ αἴσθησις μὴ ψευδὴς τοῦ γε ἰδίου ἐστίν, ἀλλʼ ἡ φαντασία οὐ ταὐτὸν τῇ αἰσθήσει. εἶτʼ ἄξιον θαυμάσαι εἰ τοῦτʼ ἀποροῦσι, πότερον τηλικαῦτά ἐστι τὰ μεγέθη καὶ τὰ χρώματα τοιαῦτα οἷα τοῖς ἄπωθεν φαίνεται ἢ οἷα τοῖς ἐγγύθεν, καὶ πότερον οἷα τοῖς ὑγιαίνουσιν ἢ οἷα τοῖς κάμνουσιν, καὶ βαρύτερα πότερον ἃ τοῖς ἀσθενοῦσιν ἢ ἃ τοῖς ἰσχύουσιν, καὶ ἀληθῆ πότερον ἃ τοῖς καθεύδουσιν ἢ ἃ τοῖς ἐγρηγορόσιν. ὅτι μὲν γὰρ οὐκ οἴονταί γε, φανερόν· οὐθεὶς γοῦν, ἐὰν ὑπολάβῃ νύκτωρ Ἀθήνῃσιν εἶναι ὢν ἐν Λιβύῃ, πορεύεται εἰς τὸ ᾠδεῖον. ἔτι δὲ περὶ τοῦ μέλλοντος, ὥσπερ καὶ Πλάτων λέγει, οὐ δήπου ὁμοίως κυρία ἡ τοῦ ἰατροῦ δόξα καὶ ἡ τοῦ ἀγνοοῦντος, οἷον περὶ τοῦ μέλλοντος ἔσεσθαι ὑγιοῦς ἢ μὴ μέλλοντος. ἔτι δὲ ἐπʼ αὐτῶν τῶν αἰσθήσεων οὐχ ὁμοίως κυρία ἡ τοῦ ἀλλοτρίου καὶ ἰδίου ἢ τοῦ πλησίον καὶ τοῦ αὑτῆς, ἀλλὰ περὶ μὲν χρώματος ὄψις, οὐ γεῦσις, περὶ δὲ χυμοῦ γεῦσις, οὐκ ὄψις· ὧν ἑκάστη ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ χρόνῳ περὶ τὸ αὐτὸ οὐδέποτε φησιν ἅμα οὕτω καὶ οὐχ οὕτως ἔχειν. ἀλλʼ οὐδὲ ἐν ἑτέρῳ χρόνῳ περί γε τὸ πάθος ἠμφισβήτησεν, ἀλλὰ περὶ τὸ ᾧ συμβέβηκε τὸ πάθος. λέγω δʼ οἷον ὁ μὲν αὐτὸς οἶνος δόξειεν ἂν ἢ μεταβαλὼν ἢ τοῦ σώματος μεταβαλόντος ὁτὲ μὲν εἶναι γλυκὺς ὁτὲ δὲ οὐ γλυκύς· ἀλλʼ οὐ τό γε γλυκύ, οἷόν ἐστιν ὅταν ᾖ, οὐδεπώποτε μετέβαλεν, ἀλλʼ ἀεὶ ἀληθεύει περὶ αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἔστιν ἐξ ἀνάγκης τὸ ἐσόμενον γλυκὺ τοιοῦτον. καίτοι τοῦτο ἀναιροῦσιν οὗτοι οἱ λόγοι ἅπαντες, ὥσπερ καὶ οὐσίαν μὴ εἶναι μηθενός, οὕτω μηδʼ ἐξ ἀνάγκης μηθέν· τὸ γὰρ ἀναγκαῖον οὐκ ἐνδέχεται ἄλλως καὶ ἄλλως ἔχειν, ὥστʼ εἴ τι ἔστιν ἐξ ἀνάγκης, οὐχ ἕξει οὕτω τε καὶ οὐχ οὕτως.—
notes: "As Plato too says": Theaetetus 171e and 178b-179a, where Socrates argues against Protagoras that about what will be, the expert's judgement is better than anyone else's. The Odeum was the concert hall at Athens, built by Pericles.

paragraphs.modern: And in general, if only the sensible is, there would be nothing if there were no living things, since there would be no sensation. That there would be neither sensible things nor sensations is perhaps true (for it is an affection of the one who senses); but that the underlying things that produce the sensation should not be, even without sensation, is impossible. For sensation is surely not of itself, but there is something else besides the sensation, which must be prior to the sensation; for what moves is prior by nature to what is moved, and none the less so if they are said with reference to each other.
paragraphs.greek: ὅλως τʼ εἴπερ ἔστι τὸ αἰσθητὸν μόνον, οὐθὲν ἂν εἴη μὴ ὄντων τῶν ἐμψύχων· αἴσθησις γὰρ οὐκ ἂν εἴη. τὸ μὲν οὖν μήτε τὰ αἰσθητὰ εἶναι μήτε τὰ αἰσθήματα ἴσως ἀληθές (τοῦ γὰρ αἰσθανομένου πάθος τοῦτό ἐστι), τὸ δὲ τὰ ὑποκείμενα μὴ εἶναι, ἃ ποιεῖ τὴν αἴσθησιν, καὶ ἄνευ αἰσθήσεως, ἀδύνατον. οὐ γὰρ δὴ ἥ γʼ αἴσθησις αὐτὴ ἑαυτῆς ἐστίν, ἀλλʼ ἔστι τι καὶ ἕτερον παρὰ τὴν αἴσθησιν, ὃ ἀνάγκη πρότερον εἶναι τῆς αἰσθήσεως· τὸ γὰρ κινοῦν τοῦ κινουμένου φύσει πρότερόν ἐστι, κἂν εἰ λέγεται πρὸς ἄλληλα ταῦτα, οὐθὲν ἧττον.
notes: What causes the sensation is prior to it, "for what moves is prior by nature to what is moved". The Platonists took the argument further: the sensible itself depends on what is prior to it, the intelligible (Proclus, on the Timaeus, Book I).

paragraphs.modern: There are some, both of those who are convinced of these things and of those who only state these arguments, who raise the puzzle of who is to judge the healthy person, and in general who is to judge rightly about each thing. Such puzzles are like being puzzled whether we are now asleep or awake. All such puzzles come to the same: these people think there should be an account of everything. They seek a starting-point, and seek to get it by proof; yet it is plain from their actions that they are not convinced. But, as we said, this is what happens to them: they seek an account of things of which there is no account, for the starting-point of proof is not proof.
paragraphs.greek: εἰσὶ δέ τινες οἳ ἀποροῦσι καὶ τῶν ταῦτα πεπεισμένων καὶ τῶν τοὺς λόγους τούτους μόνον λεγόντων· ζητοῦσι γὰρ τίς ὁ κρινῶν τὸν ὑγιαίνοντα καὶ ὅλως τὸν περὶ ἕκαστα κρινοῦντα ὀρθῶς. τὰ δὲ τοιαῦτα ἀπορήματα ὅμοιά ἐστι τῷ ἀπορεῖν πότερον καθεύδομεν νῦν ἢ ἐγρηγόραμεν, δύνανται δʼ αἱ ἀπορίαι αἱ τοιαῦται πᾶσαι τὸ αὐτό· πάντων γὰρ λόγον ἀξιοῦσιν εἶναι οὗτοι· ἀρχὴν γὰρ ζητοῦσι, καὶ ταύτην διʼ ἀποδείξεως λαμβάνειν, ἐπεὶ ὅτι γε πεπεισμένοι οὐκ εἰσί, φανεροί εἰσιν ἐν ταῖς πράξεσιν. ἀλλʼ ὅπερ εἴπομεν, τοῦτο αὐτῶν τὸ πάθος ἐστίν· λόγον γὰρ ζητοῦσιν ὧν οὐκ ἔστι λόγος· ἀποδείξεως γὰρ ἀρχὴ οὐκ ἀπόδειξίς ἐστιν. οὗτοι μὲν οὖν ῥᾳδίως ἂν τοῦτο πεισθεῖεν (ἔστι γὰρ οὐ χαλεπὸν λαβεῖν)·

paragraphs.modern: These, then, could easily be persuaded of this, since it is not hard to grasp. But those who seek only to be forced by argument seek what is impossible: they ask to be allowed to contradict themselves, and they contradict themselves from the start. But if not all things are relative, but some things are themselves by themselves, not everything that appears will be true; for what appears appears to someone; so one who says that all that appears is true makes all things relative. That is why those who seek force in argument, and at the same time want to submit to argument, must guard themselves by saying, not that what appears is, but that what appears is for the one to whom it appears, and when, and in the respect, and in the way it appears. And if they submit to argument, but not in this way, they will soon find themselves saying contrary things. For the same thing may appear to be honey to sight but not to taste, and, since we have two eyes, things may not appear the same to each, if their sight is unlike. To those who say, for the reasons given earlier, that what appears is true, and that therefore all things are likewise false and true, since things do not appear the same to everyone, nor always the same to the same person, but often contrary at the same time (for touch says there are two when the fingers are crossed, and sight says one): to these we shall say, "but not to the same sense, in the same part of it, in the same way, and at the same time", so that what appears would be true with these qualifications. But perhaps that is why those who argue not from a puzzle but for argument's sake must say, not that this is true, but that it is true for this person. And, as was said before, they must make everything relative, to opinion and to sensation, so that nothing has come to be or will be unless someone has first had an opinion about it. But if something has come to be or will be, plainly not everything is relative to opinion. Further, if a thing is one, it is relative to one thing or to a definite one; and if the same thing is both half and equal, still the equal is not relative to the double. If, then, in relation to the one who believes, man and what is believed are the same, man will not be the one who believes, but what is believed. And if each thing is to be relative to the one who believes, the one who believes will be relative to things infinite in kind.
paragraphs.greek: οἱ δʼ ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τὴν βίαν μόνον ζητοῦντες ἀδύνατον ζητοῦσιν· ἐναντία γὰρ εἰπεῖν ἀξιοῦσιν, εὐθὺς ἐναντία λέγοντες. εἰ δὲ μὴ ἔστι πάντα πρός τι, ἀλλʼ ἔνιά ἐστι καὶ αὐτὰ καθʼ αὑτά, οὐκ ἂν εἴη πᾶν τὸ φαινόμενον ἀληθές· τὸ γὰρ φαινόμενον τινί ἐστι φαινόμενον· ὥστε ὁ λέγων ἅπαντα τὰ φαινόμενα εἶναι ἀληθῆ ἅπαντα ποιεῖ τὰ ὄντα πρός τι. διὸ καὶ φυλακτέον τοῖς τὴν βίαν ἐν τῷ λόγῳ ζητοῦσιν, ἅμα δὲ καὶ ὑπέχειν λόγον ἀξιοῦσιν, ὅτι οὐ τὸ φαινόμενον ἔστιν ἀλλὰ τὸ φαινόμενον ᾧ φαίνεται καὶ ὅτε φαίνεται καὶ ᾗ καὶ ὥς. ἂν δʼ ὑπέχωσι μὲν λόγον, μὴ οὕτω δʼ ὑπέχωσι, συμβήσεται αὑτοῖς τἀναντία ταχὺ λέγειν. ἐνδέχεται γὰρ τὸ αὐτὸ κατὰ μὲν τὴν ὄψιν μέλι φαίνεσθαι τῇ δὲ γεύσει μή, καὶ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν δυοῖν ὄντοιν μὴ ταὐτὰ ἑκατέρᾳ τῇ ὄψει, ἂν ὦσιν ἀνόμοιαι· ἐπεὶ πρός γε τοὺς διὰ τὰς πάλαι εἰρημένας αἰτίας τὸ φαινόμενον φάσκοντας ἀληθὲς εἶναι, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο πάνθʼ ὁμοίως εἶναι ψευδῆ καὶ ἀληθῆ· οὔτε γὰρ ἅπασι ταὐτὰ φαίνεσθαι οὔτε ταὐτῷ ἀεὶ ταὐτά, ἀλλὰ πολλάκις τἀναντία κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν χρόνον (ἡ μὲν γὰρ ἁφὴ δύο λέγει ἐν τῇ ἐπαλλάξει τῶν δακτύλων ἡ δʼ ὄψις ἕν)·—ἀλλʼ οὔ τι τῇ αὐτῇ γε καὶ κατὰ τὸ αὐτὸ αἰσθήσει καὶ ὡσαύτως καὶ ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ χρόνῳ, ὥστε τοῦτʼ ἂν εἴη ἀληθές. ἀλλʼ ἴσως διὰ τοῦτʼ ἀνάγκη λέγειν τοῖς μὴ διʼ ἀπορίαν ἀλλὰ λόγου χάριν λέγουσιν, ὅτι οὐκ ἔστιν ἀληθὲς τοῦτο ἀλλὰ τούτῳ ἀληθές. καὶ ὥσπερ δὴ πρότερον εἴρηται, ἀνάγκη πρός τι ποιεῖν ἅπαντα καὶ πρὸς δόξαν καὶ αἴσθησιν, ὥστʼ οὔτε γέγονεν οὔτʼ ἔσται οὐθὲν μηθενὸς προδοξάσαντος. εἰ δὲ γέγονεν ἢ ἔσται, δῆλον ὅτι οὐκ ἂν εἴη ἅπαντα πρὸς δόξαν. ἔτι εἰ ἕν, πρὸς ἓν ἢ πρὸς ὡρισμένον· καὶ εἰ τὸ αὐτὸ καὶ ἥμισυ καὶ ἴσον, ἀλλʼ οὐ πρὸς τὸ διπλάσιόν γε τὸ ἴσον. πρὸς δὴ τὸ δοξάζον εἰ ταὐτὸ ἄνθρωπος καὶ τὸ δοξαζόμενον, οὐκ ἔσται ἄνθρωπος τὸ δοξάζον ἀλλὰ τὸ δοξαζόμενον. εἰ δʼ ἕκαστον ἔσται πρὸς τὸ δοξάζον, πρὸς ἄπειρα ἔσται τῷ εἴδει τὸ δοξάζον.
notes: The OCR of Ross's page has lost a few lines here (1011a26-28), where the honey and the two eyes are; the modern version follows the Greek. The crossed fingers: touch a small ball with two crossed fingers and it feels like two (Problems XXXV.10).

paragraphs.modern: Let this be enough to show that the firmest opinion of all is that opposite statements are not true at the same time; what follows for those who say they are; and why they say so. Since it is impossible for contradictories to be true of the same thing at the same time, plainly contraries cannot belong to the same thing at the same time either. For of contraries one is no less a privation, a privation of substance; and privation is the negation from some definite kind. If, then, it is impossible to affirm and deny truly at the same time, it is also impossible for contraries to belong at the same time, unless both belong in some respect, or one in some respect and the other without qualification.
paragraphs.greek: ὅτι μὲν οὖν βεβαιοτάτη δόξα πασῶν τὸ μὴ εἶναι ἀληθεῖς ἅμα τὰς ἀντικειμένας φάσεις, καὶ τί συμβαίνει τοῖς οὕτω λέγουσι, καὶ διὰ τί οὕτω λέγουσι, τοσαῦτα εἰρήσθω· ἐπεὶ δʼ ἀδύνατον τὴν ἀντίφασιν ἅμα ἀληθεύεσθαι κατὰ τοῦ αὐτοῦ, φανερὸν ὅτι οὐδὲ τἀναντία ἅμα ὑπάρχειν ἐνδέχεται τῷ αὐτῷ· τῶν μὲν γὰρ ἐναντίων θάτερον στέρησίς ἐστιν οὐχ ἧττον, οὐσίας δὲ στέρησις· ἡ δὲ στέρησις ἀπόφασίς ἐστιν ἀπό τινος ὡρισμένου γένους· εἰ οὖν ἀδύνατον ἅμα καταφάναι καὶ ἀποφάναι ἀληθῶς, ἀδύνατον καὶ τἀναντία ὑπάρχειν ἅμα, ἀλλʼ ἢ πῇ ἄμφω ἢ θάτερον μὲν πῇ θάτερον δὲ ἁπλῶς.

paragraphs.modern: But neither can there be anything between the two sides of a contradiction: of one thing one must either affirm or deny any one thing. This is plain, first, to those who define what the true and the false are. To say that what is is not, or that what is not is, is false; to say that what is is, and that what is not is not, is true; so that one who says that something is or is not will speak truly or falsely. But neither what is nor what is not is said not to be or to be. Again, what is between the contradiction will be so either as grey is between black and white, or as what is neither man nor horse is between man and horse. If in the second way, it would not change; for change is from not-good to good, or from good to not-good; but as it is, it is always seen to change, since there is no change except into opposites and what is between them. And if it is between in the first way, so too there would be a coming to be into white that is not from not-white; but as it is, this is not seen.
paragraphs.greek: ἀλλὰ μὴν οὐδὲ μεταξὺ ἀντιφάσεως ἐνδέχεται εἶναι οὐθέν, ἀλλʼ ἀνάγκη ἢ φάναι ἢ ἀποφάναι ἓν καθʼ ἑνὸς ὁτιοῦν. δῆλον δὲ πρῶτον μὲν ὁρισαμένοις τί τὸ ἀληθὲς καὶ ψεῦδος. τὸ μὲν γὰρ λέγειν τὸ ὂν μὴ εἶναι ἢ τὸ μὴ ὂν εἶναι ψεῦδος, τὸ δὲ τὸ ὂν εἶναι καὶ τὸ μὴ ὂν μὴ εἶναι ἀληθές, ὥστε καὶ ὁ λέγων εἶναι ἢ μὴ ἀληθεύσει ἢ ψεύσεται· ἀλλʼ οὔτε τὸ ὂν λέγεται μὴ εἶναι ἢ εἶναι οὔτε τὸ μὴ ὄν. ἔτι ἤτοι μεταξὺ ἔσται τῆς ἀντιφάσεως ὥσπερ τὸ φαιὸν μέλανος καὶ λευκοῦ, ἢ ὡς τὸ μηδέτερον ἀνθρώπου καὶ ἵππου. εἰ μὲν οὖν οὕτως, οὐκ ἂν μεταβάλλοι (ἐκ μὴ ἀγαθοῦ γὰρ εἰς ἀγαθὸν μεταβάλλει ἢ ἐκ τούτου εἰς μὴ ἀγαθόν), νῦν δʼ ἀεὶ φαίνεται (οὐ γὰρ ἔστι μεταβολὴ ἀλλʼ ἢ εἰς τὰ ἀντικείμενα καὶ μεταξύ)· εἰ δʼ ἔστι μεταξύ, καὶ οὕτως εἴη ἄν τις εἰς λευκὸν οὐκ ἐκ μὴ λευκοῦ γένεσις, νῦν δʼ οὐχ ὁρᾶται.

flags.taylor: To say of what is that it is not, or of what is not that it is, is false
flags.why: Ross's words are right and famous; the definition of truth they give is Aristotle's, and Plato's before him: the Sophist (240d-241a, 263b) and the Cratylus (385b) say that a true statement says the things that are as they are.

paragraphs.modern: Again, thought either affirms or denies everything that is thought or intelligible; this is plain from the definition, whenever it speaks truly or falsely. When it puts things together in this way, affirming or denying, it speaks truly; when in that way, falsely. Again, there must be something besides all contradictions, if one is not speaking just for argument's sake; so that someone will speak neither truly nor not truly, and there will be something between being and not-being, so that there will also be a kind of change between coming to be and perishing. Again, in all kinds in which the negation brings in the contrary, there will be this too: among numbers, for instance, a number neither odd nor not odd. But this is impossible, as is plain from the definition. Again, it will go on without end, and the things that are will be not only half as many again, but more. For again it will be possible to deny this, both with respect to the affirmation and to the negation, and this will be something, since its substance is something else. Again, when someone, asked whether something is white, says "no", he has denied nothing but that it is; and not being is a negation.
paragraphs.greek: ἔτι πᾶν τὸ διανοητὸν καὶ νοητὸν ἡ διάνοια ἢ κατάφησιν ἢ ἀπόφησιν—τοῦτο δʼ ἐξ ὁρισμοῦ δῆλον—ὅταν ἀληθεύῃ ἢ ψεύδηται· ὅταν μὲν ὡδὶ συνθῇ φᾶσα ἢ ἀποφᾶσα, ἀληθεύει, ὅταν δὲ ὡδί, ψεύδεται. ἔτι παρὰ πάσας δεῖ εἶναι τὰς ἀντιφάσεις, εἰ μὴ λόγου ἕνεκα λέγεται· ὥστε καὶ οὔτε ἀληθεύσει τις οὔτʼ οὐκ ἀληθεύσει, καὶ παρὰ τὸ ὂν καὶ τὸ μὴ ὂν ἔσται, ὥστε καὶ παρὰ γένεσιν καὶ φθορὰν μεταβολή τις ἔσται. ἔτι ἐν ὅσοις γένεσιν ἡ ἀπόφασις τὸ ἐναντίον ἐπιφέρει, καὶ ἐν τούτοις ἔσται, οἷον ἐν ἀριθμοῖς οὔτε περιττὸς οὔτε οὐ περιττὸς ἀριθμός· ἀλλʼ ἀδύνατον· ἐκ τοῦ ὁρισμοῦ δὲ δῆλον. ἔτι εἰς ἄπειρον βαδιεῖται, καὶ οὐ μόνον ἡμιόλια τὰ ὄντα ἔσται ἀλλὰ πλείω. πάλιν γὰρ ἔσται ἀποφῆσαι τοῦτο πρὸς τὴν φάσιν καὶ τὴν ἀπόφασιν, καὶ τοῦτʼ ἔσται τι· ἡ γὰρ οὐσία ἐστί τις αὐτοῦ ἄλλη. ἔτι ὅταν ἐρομένου εἰ λευκόν ἐστιν εἴπῃ ὅτι οὔ, οὐθὲν ἄλλο ἀποπέφηκεν ἢ τὸ εἶναι· ἀπόφασις δὲ τὸ μὴ εἶναι.

flags.taylor: the dianoetic power of the soul either affirms or denies every thing dianoetic and intelligible
flags.why: Taylor's "dianoetic" renders διάνοια and διανοητόν: thought that reasons, and what it reasons about. The Platonists set διάνοια, discursive reasoning, below νοῦς, intellect, which sees without reasoning (Republic 511d-e); here Aristotle uses the two words together for whatever is thought.

paragraphs.modern: This opinion has come to some as other paradoxes have: when they cannot answer contentious arguments, they give in to the argument and agree that the conclusion is true. Some say it for this reason, others because they seek an account of everything. The starting-point against all of them is definition; and definition comes from their having to mean something, since the account of which the name is a sign will be a definition. The argument of Heraclitus, saying that all things are and are not, seems to make all things true; that of Anaxagoras, that there is something between the contradiction, all things false: for when things are mixed, the mixture is neither good nor not good, so that nothing can be said truly.
paragraphs.greek: ἐλήλυθε δʼ ἐνίοις αὕτη ἡ δόξα ὥσπερ καὶ ἄλλαι τῶν παραδόξων· ὅταν γὰρ λύειν μὴ δύνωνται λόγους ἐριστικούς, ἐνδόντες τῷ λόγῳ σύμφασιν ἀληθὲς εἶναι τὸ συλλογισθέν. οἱ μὲν οὖν διὰ τοιαύτην αἰτίαν λέγουσιν, οἱ δὲ διὰ τὸ πάντων ζητεῖν λόγον. ἀρχὴ δὲ πρὸς ἅπαντας τούτους ἐξ ὁρισμοῦ. ὁρισμὸς δὲ γίγνεται ἐκ τοῦ σημαίνειν τι ἀναγκαῖον εἶναι αὐτούς· ὁ γὰρ λόγος οὗ τὸ ὄνομα σημεῖον ὁρισμὸς ἔσται. ἔοικε δʼ ὁ μὲν Ἡρακλείτου λόγος, λέγων πάντα εἶναι καὶ μὴ εἶναι, ἅπαντα ἀληθῆ ποιεῖν, ὁ δʼ Ἀναξαγόρου, εἶναί τι μεταξὺ τῆς ἀντιφάσεως, πάντα ψευδῆ· ὅταν γὰρ μιχθῇ, οὔτε ἀγαθὸν οὔτε οὐκ ἀγαθὸν τὸ μῖγμα, ὥστʼ οὐδὲν εἰπεῖν ἀληθές.
notes: Contentious (eristic) arguments: arguments made to win, not to find the truth, such as those of the brothers in Plato's Euthydemus. Aristotle's Sophistical Refutations shows how to answer them.

paragraphs.modern: With these distinctions drawn, it is plain that the things said in one way only, and of everything, cannot hold as some say: some say that nothing is true (for they say nothing prevents everything from being like the diagonal's being commensurable), and others that everything is true. These arguments are almost the same as that of Heraclitus: for one who says that all things are true and all false also says each of these apart, so that if they are impossible, both together must be impossible too. Again, there are plainly contradictions that cannot be true at the same time; nor all false, though this would seem more possible from what has been said. But against all such arguments one must ask, as was said in the arguments above, not that something is or is not, but that he mean something; so one must argue from a definition, taking what the false or the true means. If to say truly is nothing other than to deny falsely, it is impossible that everything be false: for one side of the contradiction must be true. Again, if one must either affirm or deny everything, both cannot be false: one side of the contradiction is false. And it happens to all such arguments, as is often said, that they destroy themselves. One who says that everything is true makes the statement contrary to his own true too, so that his own is not true (for the contrary says that it is not true); and one who says that everything is false makes himself false too. And if they make exceptions, the one saying that only the statement contrary to his is not true, and the other that only his own is not false, none the less they will be asking for infinitely many true and false statements: for the one saying that the true statement is true is true, and this will go on without end.
paragraphs.greek: διωρισμένων δὲ τούτων φανερὸν ὅτι καὶ τὰ μοναχῶς λεγόμενα καὶ κατὰ πάντων ἀδύνατον ὑπάρχειν ὥσπερ τινὲς λέγουσιν, οἱ μὲν οὐθὲν φάσκοντες ἀληθὲς εἶναι (οὐθὲν γὰρ κωλύειν φασὶν οὕτως ἅπαντα εἶναι ὥσπερ τὸ τὴν διάμετρον σύμμετρον εἶναι), οἱ δὲ πάντʼ ἀληθῆ. σχεδὸν γὰρ οὗτοι οἱ λόγοι οἱ αὐτοὶ τῷ Ἡρακλείτου· ὁ γὰρ λέγων ὅτι πάντʼ ἀληθῆ καὶ πάντα ψευδῆ, καὶ χωρὶς λέγει τῶν λόγων ἑκάτερον τούτων, ὥστʼ εἴπερ ἀδύνατα ἐκεῖνα, καὶ ταῦτα ἀδύνατον εἶναι. ἔτι δὲ φανερῶς ἀντιφάσεις εἰσὶν ἃς οὐχ οἷόν τε ἅμα ἀληθεῖς εἶναι—οὐδὲ δὴ ψευδεῖς πάσας· καίτοι δόξειέ γʼ ἂν μᾶλλον ἐνδέχεσθαι ἐκ τῶν εἰρημένων. ἀλλὰ πρὸς πάντας τοὺς τοιούτους λόγους αἰτεῖσθαι δεῖ, καθάπερ ἐλέχθη καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἐπάνω λόγοις, οὐχὶ εἶναί τι ἢ μὴ εἶναι ἀλλὰ σημαίνειν τι, ὥστε ἐξ ὁρισμοῦ διαλεκτέον λαβόντας τί σημαίνει τὸ ψεῦδος ἢ τὸ ἀληθές. εἰ δὲ μηθὲν ἄλλο τὸ ἀληθὲς φάναι ἢ ὃ ἀποφάναι ψεῦδός ἐστιν, ἀδύνατον πάντα ψευδῆ εἶναι· ἀνάγκη γὰρ τῆς ἀντιφάσεως θάτερον εἶναι μόριον ἀληθές. ἔτι εἰ πᾶν ἢ φάναι ἢ ἀποφάναι ἀναγκαῖον, ἀδύνατον ἀμφότερα ψευδῆ εἶναι· θάτερον γὰρ μόριον τῆς ἀντιφάσεως ψεῦδός ἐστιν. συμβαίνει δὴ καὶ τὸ θρυλούμενον πᾶσι τοῖς τοιούτοις λόγοις, αὐτοὺς ἑαυτοὺς ἀναιρεῖν. ὁ μὲν γὰρ πάντα ἀληθῆ λέγων καὶ τὸν ἐναντίον αὑτοῦ λόγον ἀληθῆ ποιεῖ, ὥστε τὸν ἑαυτοῦ οὐκ ἀληθῆ (ὁ γὰρ ἐναντίος οὔ φησιν αὐτὸν ἀληθῆ), ὁ δὲ πάντα ψευδῆ καὶ αὐτὸς αὑτόν. ἐὰν δʼ ἐξαιρῶνται ὁ μὲν τὸν ἐναντίον ὡς οὐκ ἀληθὴς μόνος ἐστίν, ὁ δὲ τὸν αὑτοῦ ὡς οὐ ψευδής, οὐδὲν ἧττον ἀπείρους συμβαίνει αὐτοῖς αἰτεῖσθαι λόγους ἀληθεῖς καὶ ψευδεῖς· ὁ γὰρ λέγων τὸν ἀληθῆ λόγον ἀληθῆ ἀληθής, τοῦτο δʼ εἰς ἄπειρον βαδιεῖται.—
notes: That the diagonal of a square is not commensurable with its side was the great discovery of early Greek mathematics, and Aristotle's standard example of what is impossible; Plato's Theaetetus (147d-148b) and Meno (82b-85b) are built on it.

paragraphs.modern: Plainly, too, neither those who say that all things are at rest speak truly, nor those who say that all things are in motion. If all things are at rest, the same things will always be true and false; but this plainly changes, for the one who speaks was once not and again will not be. And if all things are in motion, nothing will be true: everything, then, will be false; but it has been shown that this is impossible. Again, it must be what is that changes, since change is from something into something. But neither are all things at rest or in motion sometimes, and nothing always: for there is something that always moves the things that are moved, and the first mover is itself unmoved.
paragraphs.greek: φανερὸν δʼ ὅτι οὐδʼ οἱ πάντα ἠρεμεῖν λέγοντες ἀληθῆ λέγουσιν οὐδʼ οἱ πάντα κινεῖσθαι. εἰ μὲν γὰρ ἠρεμεῖ πάντα, ἀεὶ ταὐτὰ ἀληθῆ καὶ ψευδῆ ἔσται, φαίνεται δὲ τοῦτο μεταβάλλον (ὁ γὰρ λέγων ποτὲ αὐτὸς οὐκ ἦν καὶ πάλιν οὐκ ἔσται)· εἰ δὲ πάντα κινεῖται, οὐθὲν ἔσται ἀληθές· πάντα ἄρα ψευδῆ· ἀλλὰ δέδεικται ὅτι ἀδύνατον. ἔτι ἀνάγκη τὸ ὂν μεταβάλλειν· ἔκ τινος γὰρ εἴς τι ἡ μεταβολή. ἀλλὰ μὴν οὐδὲ πάντα ἠρεμεῖ ἢ κινεῖται ποτέ, ἀεὶ δʼ οὐθέν· ἔστι γάρ τι ὃ ἀεὶ κινεῖ τὰ κινούμενα, καὶ τὸ πρῶτον κινοῦν ἀκίνητον αὐτό.

flags.taylor: and the first mover must itself be unmoved
flags.why: Ross's words are right; the note is the Platonists'. The first unmoved mover is the subject of Book Λ (chapters 6 to 9) and of Physics VIII. For the Platonists Aristotle's first mover is intellect, which they set below the One, as Plato's maker of the world in the Timaeus looks to what is above him.
